passage: Friday night. Three videos this week showed young people with fancy phones saying they earn from trading and paid schemes with no skill needed. Today I joined a group, paid the entry fee from my savings, and told nobody, not even Gargi, because she would ask questions. The people in the group post screenshots of gains, and I am not sure which are real. I still don't understand how anyone earns, only that I have to bring in two friends to unlock the next level. I lost a full afternoon watching the group chat instead of studying. I don't feel excited anymore. I feel foolish. Tomorrow I will stop paying anything more and speak to my parents. Nandini

qa.q: What did Nandini pay for from savings?
qa.a: Nandini paid the entry fee for the group from savings.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel by the end of the entry?
qa.a: Nandini no longer felt excited and felt foolish, and had lost an afternoon watching the group chat.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Nandini have used before joining, and why?
qa.a: Nandini could have asked how the money was actually earned and talked to Gargi or a parent first, because real earnings can be explained plainly.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel if she learned Nandini had told her nothing?
qa.a: Gargi may feel worried and a bit hurt, since she would have asked the questions that could have stopped the joining.

grounding: A student joins a scheme from videos claiming easy earnings without checking, risking savings and time and learning no real skill.

passage:
At the Phaltan bus stand tea stall, there was one topic that month: phone videos of a young man showing off a new bike, 'all from an earning app'. Omkar, in his second year at the local college, watched them on Vishal's phone while waiting for the 4:15 bus.
'Joining is ₹1,500,' Vishal said. 'Then you bring two people.'
Omkar paid from the money he'd saved weighing sugarcane at the factory gate over the holidays. For three weeks he spent his evenings messaging classmates, cousins, even the tailor, instead of studying for his diploma exam. Two people joined. The app showed ₹900 in his 'wallet', which he could never withdraw.
The week results came out, the app stopped opening. Omkar sat at the stall, turning his phone over in his hand. He had lost the fee, three weeks and a few friendships, and he still could not say what the app actually did.

qa.q: How much was the joining fee?
What might Omkar be feeling as he sits at the stall turning his phone over?
qa.a: He is likely ashamed and hollow, counting what he lost, including friendships, and uneasy that he never understood the app.

qa.q: What else could Omkar have done with those three weeks of evenings?
qa.a: He could have asked a college teacher about genuine local part-time work, or built on a skill he already had, instead of paying into something he never checked.

qa.q: What is it like for the classmates and cousins Omkar messaged?
qa.a: They were pressed to join something he could not explain, and the two who joined probably lost money too, which strains their trust in him.

grounding: Shows a young man copying others into a paid earning scheme without checking, losing savings, study time and friendships while learning no skill.
